A haptic response may be controlled by first receiving a force signal from a force sensor. The force signal is analyzed to determine an associated force magnitude, which represents the amount of force being applied by a user.

The determined force magnitude is then compared with an initial threshold value. This comparison is used to determine whether the applied force exceeds a required force amount. If the force magnitude does not exceed the threshold, the system may take no further action or may continue monitoring the force signal.

When the force magnitude exceeds the initial threshold, the system measures the amount of time during which the force magnitude remains above that threshold. This elapsed time is compared with a minimum elapsed time requirement. The purpose of this comparison is to ensure that the detected force is intentional and sustained, rather than brief or accidental.

If the elapsed time exceeds the minimum elapsed time, the system generates a haptic feedback control signal. The haptic feedback control signal causes a haptic actuator to propagate pressure waves. The frequency of the propagated pressure waves is proportional to the detected force magnitude, so that a greater applied force may result in a higher haptic propagation frequency.

In addition, a scroll control signal is generated to control a menu system. The scroll control signal causes the menu system to scroll through available menu options at a frequency associated with the haptic propagation frequency. As a result, the scrolling behavior of the menu system is coordinated with the haptic feedback provided to the user.
outputs.L4:
A haptic control method may be used to provide force-responsive tactile feedback during operation of an electronic device, such as a touch-sensitive display, control surface, wearable device, handheld terminal, or other user interface. The method receives an input signal from a force sensor that detects a force applied by a user to an input region. Based on the sensor signal, the system determines a magnitude of the applied force and compares the determined force magnitude with a preset threshold value. If the applied force does not exceed the threshold, the system may refrain from generating haptic feedback or may continue operating in a normal input mode.

When the applied force exceeds the threshold, the system measures an elapsed time during which the force remains above the threshold. Haptic feedback is generated only when the force magnitude has exceeded the threshold for at least a predetermined minimum time period. This delay helps prevent accidental activation caused by brief touches, noise, or unintended pressure changes. If the force drops below the threshold before the minimum time elapses, the system may reset the timing operation and withhold the haptic response.

After the threshold and timing conditions are satisfied, the system generates pressure-wave haptic feedback. The pressure-wave feedback may be delivered through an actuator, vibration element, ultrasonic element, piezoelectric element, or another haptic output device. The frequency of the generated pressure-wave feedback is controlled according to the magnitude of the detected force. For example, a greater applied force may produce a higher feedback frequency, while a smaller force above the threshold may produce a lower feedback frequency. In this way, the user receives tactile information that corresponds to the amount of force being applied.

The method may also coordinate the haptic feedback with movement of a graphical user interface, such as a menu, list, selector, or scrolling display. When the pressure-wave haptic feedback is active, the frequency of menu scrolling is synchronized with the frequency of the haptic feedback. As the user presses harder, both the tactile feedback frequency and the scrolling frequency may increase; as the user reduces pressure, both frequencies may decrease. This synchronization allows the user to perceive menu navigation through touch as well as visually, improving control precision and enabling intuitive force-based navigation.

By requiring both a force threshold and a minimum elapsed time before activation, the method reduces unintended haptic output while preserving responsiveness. By varying the haptic frequency in proportion to force magnitude and synchronizing the menu scrolling frequency with the haptic output, the method provides a tactile interface in which pressure directly controls navigation speed and feedback intensity. The result is a force-responsive haptic control technique that can improve user interaction with menus, lists, and other selectable interface elements.

## Implementations

Implementations are the practical steps taken to turn ideas, plans, designs, or strategies into working solutions. While planning defines what should be done, implementation focuses on how it is actually carried out. This can apply to many areas, including technology, business, education, healthcare, government policy, and project management.

In software development, implementations refer to the process of writing code based on a design, specification, or algorithm. For example, a developer may implement a payment system, a search feature, or a security protocol. A successful implementation must be reliable, efficient, scalable, and easy to maintain.

In business, implementations often involve putting new strategies, tools, or processes into action. This may include introducing a new customer relationship management system, launching a marketing campaign, or restructuring internal workflows. Effective implementation requires clear goals, communication, training, and ongoing evaluation.

Good implementations usually follow several key stages. First, the requirements and objectives must be clearly understood. Next, a detailed plan is created, including timelines, responsibilities, and resources. After that, the solution is developed or introduced, tested, and adjusted as needed. Finally, the implementation is monitored to ensure it delivers the expected results.

One of the main challenges of implementations is managing change. Even a strong idea can fail if people are not prepared to use it or if the process is poorly organized. For this reason, communication, stakeholder involvement, and feedback are essential.

Overall, implementations are where concepts become reality. They bridge the gap between planning and results, making them a critical part of innovation, growth, and problem-solving in any field.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style "implementations include" paragraph describing a method for controlling haptic feedback and menu scrolling based on force sensor input.
counterfactuals.output: Implementations include a method comprising receiving, from one or more force sensors coupled to an input surface of an electronic device, force data indicative of a magnitude, location, rate of change, and/or duration of a user-applied force; determining, based at least in part on the force data, whether the user-applied force satisfies one or more force criteria associated with a menu navigation operation; in response to determining that a first force threshold is satisfied, initiating scrolling of a displayed menu in a first direction or at a first scrolling rate; modifying the scrolling rate, scrolling acceleration, or item-by-item advancement of the displayed menu based on changes in the magnitude or rate of change of the user-applied force; generating, by a haptic output device, haptic feedback corresponding to the menu navigation operation, the haptic feedback including at least one of a detent sensation, vibration pulse, click sensation, or resistance simulation associated with traversal of one or more menu items; and, in response to determining that the user-applied force satisfies a second force threshold, selecting a highlighted menu item, changing a scrolling mode, increasing or decreasing haptic intensity, or terminating the scrolling operation. In some implementations, the method further includes filtering the force data to reject unintended inputs, calibrating the force thresholds based on user preferences or device orientation, and synchronizing the haptic feedback with visual movement of the displayed menu such that each menu item transition is accompanied by a corresponding haptic effect.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a legalistic technical description of a haptic response control method involving force magnitude thresholds, elapsed-time validation, actuator pressure waves, and proportional menu scrolling.
counterfactuals.output:
A haptic response control method is provided for an electronic device having a touch-sensitive input surface, a processor, a display, and at least one haptic actuator configured to impart a tactile output to the input surface or to a housing of the electronic device.

The method comprises detecting, by the processor, a user input applied to the touch-sensitive input surface, the user input being associated with a measured force magnitude. The processor compares the measured force magnitude with at least one predetermined force magnitude threshold. In response to determining that the measured force magnitude satisfies a first force magnitude threshold condition, the processor initiates an elapsed-time validation procedure. The elapsed-time validation procedure includes determining whether the user input continuously satisfies the first force magnitude threshold condition for at least a predetermined validation interval, thereby distinguishing an intentional force-based command from a transient contact, tap artifact, or incidental pressure variation.

Upon validating that the measured force magnitude has satisfied the first force magnitude threshold condition for the predetermined validation interval, the processor generates a haptic control signal corresponding to a first haptic response. The haptic control signal is provided to the at least one haptic actuator to produce one or more pressure waves, mechanical pulses, vibrotactile impulses, or force-feedback events perceptible to the user. In certain implementations, the pressure waves are generated with an amplitude, duration, frequency, waveform, or pulse count selected according to the measured force magnitude, the duration of the applied force, the rate of change of the force magnitude, or a selected user-interface state.

The method further comprises determining whether the measured force magnitude satisfies a second force magnitude threshold condition different from the first force magnitude threshold condition. In response to satisfaction of the second force magnitude threshold condition, and optionally upon completion of a second elapsed-time validation interval, the processor generates a second haptic control signal distinct from the first haptic control signal. The second haptic control signal causes the haptic actuator to generate a second actuator pressure wave pattern, thereby indicating to the user that a different force-input state or command level has been reached.

In an implementation involving a graphical menu, the method further comprises controlling scrolling of menu items displayed on the display in proportion to the measured force magnitude. A scroll rate, scroll distance, acceleration value, or incremental menu displacement is determined as a function of the amount by which the measured force magnitude exceeds a baseline value or one of the predetermined force magnitude thresholds. Accordingly, a relatively lower applied force produces a slower or smaller menu-scrolling response, while a relatively higher applied force produces a faster or larger menu-scrolling response. The processor may continuously update the menu-scrolling response while the user input remains detected, such that the displayed menu movement is dynamically proportional to the current force magnitude.

The method may further include suppressing generation of the haptic response when the measured force magnitude fails to remain above the applicable threshold for the required validation interval. The method may also include terminating or attenuating the actuator pressure waves when the measured force magnitude falls below a release threshold, when the input contact is removed, or when a maximum haptic output duration is reached. Hysteresis may be applied between activation and release thresholds to reduce oscillation or repeated triggering caused by minor variations in measured force.

In one embodiment, the processor stores a plurality of force magnitude thresholds, each associated with a respective elapsed-time requirement, haptic actuator waveform, and menu-scrolling parameter. The processor selects among the stored thresholds based on an active application, a displayed menu type, user preference data, device orientation, or detected input location. The resulting tactile output provides confirmation of force-level transitions, while the proportional scrolling behavior enables continuous navigation through the menu without requiring repeated discrete touch gestures.

Thus, the method provides force-sensitive haptic feedback in which actuator pressure waves are generated only after threshold satisfaction and elapsed-time validation, and in which menu scrolling is controlled in a proportional relationship to applied force magnitude.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in patent application language, a system that detects sustained force above an initial threshold and uses it to control both haptic actuator propagation frequency and menu scroll frequency.
counterfactuals.output:
A system is provided for controlling an electronic device based on detection of a sustained force input. The system may include a force-sensitive input surface, one or more haptic actuators, a display, and control circuitry operatively coupled to the force-sensitive input surface, the one or more haptic actuators, and the display.

In one embodiment, the force-sensitive input surface is configured to generate force data indicative of a magnitude of a user-applied force. The control circuitry is configured to compare the force data to an initial force threshold. In response to determining that the user-applied force exceeds the initial force threshold, the control circuitry initiates a sustained-force detection mode. During the sustained-force detection mode, the control circuitry determines whether the user-applied force remains above the initial force threshold for at least a predetermined dwell period, or otherwise satisfies a sustained-force condition.

Upon detection of the sustained-force condition, the control circuitry controls a haptic actuator propagation frequency based at least in part on the magnitude, duration, or variation of the sustained force. The haptic actuator propagation frequency may correspond to a rate at which haptic output events, pulses, vibrations, traveling haptic waveforms, or actuator activation patterns are generated or propagated through one or more haptic actuators. For example, as the detected force increases above the initial threshold, the control circuitry may increase the propagation frequency of haptic feedback. Conversely, as the detected force decreases while remaining above the initial threshold, the control circuitry may decrease the propagation frequency.

The control circuitry is further configured to control a menu scroll frequency based at least in part on the same sustained-force input. The menu scroll frequency may correspond to a rate at which items, rows, icons, pages, options, or other menu elements are advanced, traversed, highlighted, or scrolled on the display. In some embodiments, the menu scroll frequency is varied in coordination with the haptic actuator propagation frequency, such that haptic feedback events are temporally associated with corresponding menu scrolling events. For instance, each menu advancement may be accompanied by a haptic pulse, or a plurality of haptic pulses may be generated at a frequency proportional to the scroll rate.

In certain embodiments, the control circuitry maps a force value above the initial threshold to both the haptic actuator propagation frequency and the menu scroll frequency using a common transfer function, lookup table, gain schedule, or dynamically adjustable control profile. The mapping may include one or more force bands, such that a first force range above the initial threshold produces a first haptic propagation frequency and a first menu scroll frequency, while a second, higher force range produces a second haptic propagation frequency and a second menu scroll frequency. The second frequencies may be greater than the first frequencies.

The system may also include filtering logic configured to distinguish sustained force from transient touch events, taps, accidental contacts, or noise. The filtering logic may require that the force remain above the initial threshold for a minimum time interval, remain within a permitted force variation range, or maintain a force-time integral above a predetermined value. In response to the force falling below the initial threshold, or below a release threshold associated with hysteresis, the control circuitry may terminate the sustained-force detection mode and cease or reduce both haptic actuator propagation and menu scrolling.

In an example implementation, a user presses on a touch-sensitive display or force-sensitive control region. When the applied force exceeds the initial threshold, the system determines whether the press is sustained. Once the sustained-force condition is met, the system begins scrolling through a menu and generating haptic feedback. Increasing the applied force increases both the rate at which the menu scrolls and the frequency at which haptic feedback is propagated. The haptic output thereby provides tactile confirmation of the scroll frequency and allows the user to perceive menu traversal without requiring continuous visual attention.

In some embodiments, the haptic actuator propagation frequency and the menu scroll frequency are synchronized, phase-aligned, ratio-locked, or otherwise correlated. In other embodiments, the frequencies are independently derived from the sustained force but constrained to maintain a perceptible relationship. For example, the haptic propagation frequency may be equal to the menu scroll frequency, an integer multiple thereof, or a fractional multiple thereof.

The control circuitry may include one or more processors executing instructions stored in memory. The instructions, when executed, cause the system to: receive force sensor data; detect that an applied force exceeds an initial threshold; determine that the applied force is sustained; determine at least one control parameter based on the sustained force; generate haptic actuator control signals having a propagation frequency based on the control parameter; and generate menu navigation control signals having a scroll frequency based on the control parameter.

Accordingly, the system enables a single sustained force input above an initial threshold to control both tactile feedback timing and menu navigation speed, thereby providing coordinated force-based interaction with an electronic device.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an abstract-style implementation statement for a force-sensitive user interface that produces haptic feedback and scrolls menu options based on the applied force.
counterfactuals.output: A force-sensitive user interface is implemented using a pressure-responsive input surface coupled to a controller and a haptic actuator. The input surface detects an amount of force applied by a user and generates a corresponding force signal. The controller compares the detected force with one or more predefined force thresholds and controls navigation through a displayed menu based on the detected force level. A lower applied force may cause slow scrolling or single-step movement through menu options, while a higher applied force may cause faster scrolling, continuous scrolling, or accelerated navigation. The controller further drives the haptic actuator to generate tactile feedback corresponding to menu interaction events, force thresholds, scrolling speed, or selection states. The haptic feedback may include vibrations, pulses, resistance sensations, or other tactile responses to indicate that a force level has been recognized or that a menu option has been highlighted or selected. In this manner, the interface enables force-based menu navigation while providing physical feedback to improve user awareness and control.
